content.text:
**Potentially yes—for review classification and evidence selection.** I’d test Jev on those tasks before replacing Reviq’s current chat implementation.

The linked [[REDACTED UNRELATED HOST] site]([REDACTED UNRELATED URL] identifies itself as an unofficial community resource. [TypeSafe’s official pricing]([REDACTED UNRELATED URL] lists **$0.042 per million input tokens, with free output**. That’s about **48× cheaper for uncached input** than Reviq’s current GPT-4.1 model; overall application savings would depend on the work it replaces. [GPT-4.1 pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4.1)

| Reviq task | Potential benefit |
|---|---|
| Sentiment and predefined topic tagging | Good fit for structured decisions |
| Selecting relevant reviews | Promising: Jev selects IDs; our code displays original text |
| Writing conversational answers | Requires a text-generating model; Jev returns choices, scores and probabilities |
| Live scraping | No direct improvement to fetching pages or available review coverage |

These capabilities follow Jev’s [official API documentation]([REDACTED UNRELATED URL]

**My recommendation:** pilot evidence selection first. Reviq already emphasizes exact quotations, so selecting source IDs and rendering their original text could lower costs and avoid quote-formatting errors. Keep PostgreSQL, Apache, the scraper and source-validation checks.

Adding Jev to every question without reducing the existing GPT work would add cost and latency. We should compare answer quality, citation correctness, total cost and response time on the same review fixtures. **I haven’t benchmarked Jev against Reviq yet.**
I’ll continue with the current setup and verify that the live app and GitHub release are healthy.
